title: Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha
claim: Oak interprets the omen as an ordering of Alcor and Mizar across the meridian. He reports an interval from 11,091 to 4,508 BCE.
limit: The interval spans millennia. The local prereview run models this single interpretation and remains sensitive to the stellar inputs.

title: Bhīṣma’s death and the seasons
claim: Oak groups the duration, seasonal and calendrical terms at Bhīṣma’s death and gives roughly 7,000 to 3,700 BCE for his reading.
limit: This range reports Oak’s reasoning. Each duration and seasonal rule needs its own reproduction and textual review.

title: The war month and waxing Moon
claim: Oak combines descriptions and comparisons about the season and Moon to argue for the bright half of Mārgaśīrṣa in Śarad, with an approximate latest threshold of 4,000 BCE.
limit: Month and season conventions matter. The reported threshold is broader than the two preceding ranges when all three are selected.

title: Planet descriptions and comparisons
claim: Oak discusses observations and similes involving planets, and labels some comparisons as weaker than others. His 2019 list gives examples and his own assessments.
limit: A simile needs a defensible translation and a measurement rule before it can filter candidate dates. No planet filter is applied here.
locator: Additional astronomy evidence, with Saiswaroopa Iyer’s leads

title: Eclipse language and the Jayadratha scene
claim: The Bhīṣma book includes descriptions of obscuration. In the Jayadratha episode, Ganguli’s translation instead describes darkness brought about through yoga.
limit: These passages have different narrative settings. A proposed local eclipse needs a candidate date, geometry and Earth-rotation assumptions before it can be assessed.

title: Dwarka below the water
claim: Oak lists oceanographic corroboration for his proposed loss of Dvārakā. Marine archaeology reports finds off modern Dwarka.
limit: The age and context of a marine find need to be established separately from the epic’s account. No date filter is applied here.

title: The Rakhigarhi genome
claim: Oak lists genetics as corroboration. Shinde and colleagues published one Harappan genome from Rakhigarhi and used it to investigate population ancestry.
limit: The study dates archaeological context and analyses ancestry. It supplies no independently dated link from this person to the narrated war.

title: Ancient DNA across South and Central Asia
claim: Narasimhan and colleagues compared ancient genomes at many sites to study ancestry and population movement over time.
limit: A population model operates on groups and time ranges. This study supplies no identifiable sample from a named epic person or battlefield.

title: Sarasvatī and changing rivers
claim: Oak lists hydrology as corroboration. The route and age of a palaeochannel answer geological questions about a physical feature.
limit: A specific river identification and link to a scene need separate evidence. No date filter is applied here.

title: The Hastināpura excavation
claim: Lal’s excavation records a Painted Grey Ware occupation and a break in the archaeological sequence at modern Hastināpura.
limit: A dated occupation layer requires an independent link to an epic event before it can filter a war date.
locator: B. B. Lal, Ancient India 10–11, excavation report

title: Why 5561 BCE?
claim: Oak proposes 16 October 5561 BCE in the proleptic Julian calendar and argues for a specific year using his broader catalogue.
limit: The broad intervals above do not single out one year. Readers can inspect the proposal while individual tests and the historical review are open.
